Threat.value: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

vignette: Kai'olu, a 53-year-old married airline pilot of Pacific Islander descent, had always taken pride in his ability to remain calm under pressure. That was before the torture he endured during a layover in a foreign country several years ago. The memory of those hours still feels like an open wound, refusing to heal. It started with a sudden arrest and detention by local authorities. Kai'olu remembers the smell of sweat and diesel fuel as he was dragged away from his hotel. He recalls the sound of laughter and jeering as he was thrown into a cell. But most vividly, he remembers the feeling of helplessness as he was subjected to physical and psychological torment. In the aftermath, Kai'olu began to notice changes in himself. He would become uneasy in crowded places, like airports or shopping malls, where he felt trapped and vulnerable. The sound of crying, whether from a child or an adult, could send him into a tailspin of anxiety. And when people around him misbehaved – even something as minor as littering or cutting in line – Kai'olu would feel a surge of anger and disgust. As time went on, these reactions became more pronounced. Kai'olu found himself repeatedly checking that doors and windows were locked before he could relax at home. He'd scan the faces of strangers on the street, searching for signs of malice or deceit. Even in quiet moments, like during a solo flight or late at night in bed, an unusual silence would make him feel like something was off – like danger lurked just around the corner. Kai'olu's memories of the torture still came flooding back, often triggered by the smallest things. A whiff of diesel fuel might transport him back to that cell, where he'd relive the terror and humiliation all over again. When this happened, his mind would feel like a slideshow of photographs – vivid, intense, and impossible to escape. The emotions would overwhelm him, forcing him to shut down and retreat from the world. As these symptoms accumulated, Kai'olu began to withdraw from his loved ones and his job. He stopped attending social gatherings with his wife's family, citing exhaustion or stress. He'd arrive early for flights just so he could inspect the aircraft before anyone else boarded – a ritual that brought him some fleeting sense of control. His marriage suffered as he became increasingly irritable and distant. One day, Kai'olu realized he couldn't keep living like this. A particularly harrowing flashback during a flight had left him shaken, and his wife's concerned expression when he arrived home had finally broken through his defenses. He knew he needed help – not just to cope with these symptoms but to confront the darkness that had taken hold of his life. As Kai'olu prepares to seek treatment, he's most afraid of losing himself in this sea of anxiety and anger. What if he can't find a way back to the man he used to be? He hopes, more than anything, to learn how to quiet the constant threat monitor in his mind – to find some measure of peace and trust again in himself and those around him.
